subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED POSTAGE RATE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, millions of Canadians have finished filing this year's income tax returns. They sent their tax forms in by the April 30 deadline.
However, one businessman in northwestern Saskatchewan was waiting for a receipt he required to complete his tax form. The receipt that he needed was mailed from Toronto, postmarked March 13. He waited and he waited. Finally the receipt arrived in Battleford, Saskatchewan, 49 days later, on May 1, one day after the tax deadline.
At a time when many Canadians are growing increasingly frustrated with their Post Office, and while this same Post Office asks Canadian citizens and businesses to pay more for their postage, many ask why. I urge the Cabinet to consider very carefully the increase in postal rates requested by the Post Office.
The cost of mail is significant, particularly for small businesses. The public would not be expected to shoulder the burden of removing the deficit of a Crown corporation that sometimes provides questionable service. If the Post Office does not perform adequately, then Canadians should not have to pay more for less.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Quebec native women I make the following statement.
Indian women have had enough of the Government of Canada's refusing them the most fundamental of human rights. Indian women seek justice which they have never known since the arrival of the Indian Act in 1869. There have been one hundred years of misfortune for and injustice to those who married a non-Indian. This law, which was imposed on
them by a non-Indian government, puts control on their most fundamental human rights, and creates divisions within their families.
For those who have married a non-Indian, this law takes away their identity, the possibility of transmitting this identity to their children, the right to live in their communities, and even the right to be buried within their communities. By this same law, which comes from the federal Government, nonIndian women who marry Indian men acquire Indian status.
The federal Government, in an effort to repair these injustices, finally introduced a bill, Bill C-31, which could have re-established the full rights of Indian women and their children. However, the committee which was mandated to study this Bill has proposed amendments which are contrary to the spirit of the Bill by putting limitations on the rights of Indian women, and has refused to consider amendments which would have guaranteed the right of Indian identity for their children.
They have had enough. They insist that justice be rendered to them. They insist that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) act now. Bill C-31 must ensure full rights to women and their children.

subsubtopic: REINSTITUTION OF SERVICE BETWEEN EDMONTON AND VANCOUVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada recently took steps to reinstitute regular western VIA Rail service between Edmonton and Vancouver, which includes the scenic and much travelled tourist corridor between Jasper and Kamloops, British Columbia.
This decision enabled the local communities to develop local tourism infrastructure projects. The critical component in this long awaited development process is the existing passenger train stations in the communities located within this corridor. However, VIA and CN are considering closing stations at Valemount, Blue River, and Clearwater, which woud seriously inhibit these communities in their tourism development.
Therefore I urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazan-kowski) to intervene and take whatever action is necessary to ensure that these stations remain intact so that passengers travelling along this scenic corridor will have the opportunity to access local tourist areas, which will enhance not only VIA's attractiveness but help provide local economic development and jobs.

May 8, 1985

Mr. Speaker, what happens to Mirabel Airport will have a vital impact on the economy of the Montreal area and that of the rest of Quebec.
The Government ought to decide as soon as possible what it intends to do about Mirabel. Several Members of this House are concerned about what the Government will decide, and 1 think it is entirely unacceptable that the Government should refuse to announce whether it will approve expansion of the airport in Toronto or try to give Mirabel a certain status.
All parties concerned in this matter agree that Mirabel is the perfect location for an international airport, that it and is well suited to future expansion. There are no obstacles to expanding Mirabel, except the Government's inertia which is preventing it from making a decision. The people of Quebec and Montreal are waiting for a decision by the Government, and I think this Government is demonstrating its indifference to their expectations.

Mr. Speaker, there has been a lot of attention paid recently to the so-called Grand Canal proposal, whereby the theory is that James Bay would be dammed, turned into a freshwater lake, and water diverted back south into and beyond the Great Lakes to points in the United States.
This proposal, earlier regarded as too bizarre to be accorded much credibility, has been given some credibility lately by the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) approval of water exports by tanker from his own riding, and his subsequent silence on the broader issue of water diversion for export which the Grand Canal project raises. Perhaps the silence is intended to complement the promotion of the Grand Canal scheme by the Prime Minister's old friend, Quebec Liberal Leader Robert Bourassa, whose enthusiasm for this massive act of technological hubris and ecological insanity seems to know no bounds.
The federal Liberal caucus, on the other hand, speaks with two voices. The Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) thinks it is a great idea, while the Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) appears to be against it. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) thinks it should be studied.
Canadian waters are not ours to sell. In this sense, opposition to such a diversion is not to be seen as selfishness but as good stewardship of that which has been entrusted to us and of the ecological and planetary context in which our Arctic and northern waters need to be considered.
Americans, like Canadians, should look first to what can be done in terms of water quality improvement and water conservation. They would be surprised what we could do if the political will were there on both sides of the border. Unfortunately it does not seem to exist at this time.

Native communications societies throughout Canada are suffering a severe hiatus because of the Government's failure to date to approve any form of advance funding for the 1985-86 fiscal year.
These societies perform a valuable and essential function for native Canadians, and enrich the ethnocultural mosaic for all of us.
If present uncertainties are allowed to continue, the state of anxiety and confusion permeating the directors and staff will deepen, impairing further their effectiveness and enthusiasm.
The Government must learn to play fair with the agencies it funds. Delay is a form of denial. Numerous bodies wonder if it
May 8, 1985

is being used now to identify those programs which could later be cut without too much political backlash. It is time for the Government to put its money where the Prime Minister's April 18 statement directs.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday in a speech to the Ottawa Social Planning Council, the Executive Director of the Canadian Council on Social Development cautioned Canadians about the role that small business could play in developing long-term employment and economic opportunities. Let me say I disagree, and I point to the facts.
For the past ten years over 70 per cent of new job creation in this country has been in the small business sector. Small business is responsible for 40 per cent of all employment, and for between 55 per cent and 60 per cent of private sector employment. Women now own 29 per cent of small businesses and are creating small businesses at three times the rate of men. Small business is also the largest employer of the youth of our country.
Yes, small business may not pay the highest wages, have long-term pensions, and job security, but Canadians with ideas and independence seek out the small business sector to fulfil their dreams. Many of the innovations and new products of our society are founded in garages or small laboratories, and grow into thriving small enterprises.
I can assure Canadians that this Government stands solidly behind the small business sector. Challenge '85 is a good example. We will continue to review our policies and laws, whether in the fields of taxation, pension reform, or encouragement of our financial institutions to meet the needs of small enterprises, to respond and to enhance the future contribution of small business to create jobs and keep the Canadian economy growing.

The Hon. Member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, in answer to one of my questions, the Minister responsible for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation said that I was not familiar with the programs I had mentioned to him. In Hansard, I mentioned to the Minister the "Programme canadien de renovation et de construction de logement locatif et de logement social". I realize the Minister is not familiar with the French language, so I
Presence in Gallery
suggest he check the briefing papers provided by his Department. In English, the "regime de construction de logement locatifs" is: Canada Rental Supply Plan, and "logement social" is Social Housing.
Mr. Speaker, I would therefore suggest that the Minister brush up on his programs before answering questions, so that he can give the right answers.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today on the occasion of the fortieth anniversary of the ending of hostilities in Europe during World War II. For a great many Canadians, this day holds a special significance. It is a time for both remembrance and reflection.
Canadians have always played a vital role in the defence of democracy and freedom. Over half a million Canadians served overseas during the Second World War, most of them in Europe. From the submarine war in the Atlantic, to the Battle for Britain in the skies, to the liberation of the Netherlands, Canadians fought for the values and liberties that we now cherish so dearly.
The conflict in Europe, like all wars, was a terrible human tragedy for everyone involved; for those who went overseas, for their loved ones who endured many anxious years in Canada, and especially for those who suffered the supreme sacrifice and were never to see their homes again.
It is our duty as a civilized nation to ensure that no Canadian will ever have to endure what our brave veterans so unselfishly suffered for their country. If there is a lesson to be learned in our wartime experience in Europe, it would be to underline the need to commit ourselves to the peaceful resolution of conflict.

subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF VE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 40 years ago the war ended in Europe. This was a day of great significance because it represented a victory over the most pernicious evil ever known to man, Naziism. Naziism and its horrible work against humanity in general and the Jewish people in particular are and forever shall be an indelible stain on the conscience of history. For all those who died, this is a day of remembrance but it is also a day of hope and reconciliation and renewal.

Today we are commemorating the dedication of these Canadian men and women and the sacrifices they made. We remember especially those wives who lost their husbands and families that lost their loved ones in the war. Their sacrifice has made subsequent generations of Canadians realize that peace is our fundamental concern.
By participating in the World War, Canadians helped to liberate Europe. It is our duty today to work unceasingly for
peace, on behalf of a generation of Canadians who died in combat.

In 1939, Canada entered the war immediately, convinced that our freedom and the Freedom of future generations had been gravely and perhaps fatally jeopardized by actions taken in Europe.
Although our population was relatively small at the time, Canada committed all its resources and a million people, all of whom performed with courage and sacrifice. Many were wounded, thousands were killed, the glory of our youth consigned to European soil. Those who returned did so having paid a very high price. It is to all of them-our veterans and their families-who served this country that Canada owes its greatest and its eternal debt of gratitude.

Some who returned are in this House today in all political Parties. One of those young Canadians who went to fight, as did those from other political persuasions, with the very clear vision of what he was fighting for-and he has preserved that belief in democracy and freedom, undimmed and undiminished today-is the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen). Because of his very distinguished record of service in the greatest of wars, I invite him to speak now to Parliament on behalf of the Government of Canada.

-it was only nine days after the invasion of Poland that this House of Commons 45 years ago, without a single dissenting voice, declared war on the totalitarian state that brought it about. Before it was over there were 57 countries around the world involved on one side or the other.
A mobilization was seen here at home in Canada, the like of which has never been seen before in that kind of cause and hopefully will never be seen again. A navy was created in 1910 which, because of the foresight of the planners of the early twenties and thirties, was ready to go to meet the crisis at once and grew to be the third largest navy in the world; an air force was created in 1924 that was the scene of one of the greatest air training plans that the world has ever seen, turning out pilots from every Commonwealth country and others that were engaged in that conflict; we had an army whose roots reached deep into the past history of this country.
Today, ironically, as we move into this period of reconciliation that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spoke of, we have now as our staunch allies those who were enemies during that conflict of 40 years ago.
May 8, 1985

VE Day

subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF VE DAY
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
If the House might permit me for a moment to focus on some of the words of the Prime Minister with respect to the reason for Canadians going to war, there appears to be an impression in some quarters that those who left their farms and factories, their books and their futures in 1939, 1940 and after, had no clear idea what they were fighting for. I want to tell you, Sir, that that was not the case. You do not mobilize millions of men and women in a cause in free countries around the world without a very powerful motivation. Most of us knew precisely what we were fighting for.
As the Prime Minister mentioned, there are men and women in this House who served. The present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) is in Europe today participating in the commemorative services there to mark this occasion. The distinguished Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) and the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), who sit with us today, knew exactly what they were fighting for. Nor can we forget the role that was played by
50,000	women and the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who contributed as effectively and as fully on the home front as those of us who were there.
To say that those who took part in this tremendous conflict, this tremendous outpouring of blood and resources that was the Second World War, did not have a clear idea of what it was about is to betray that for which they fought: the right to choose our own form of government, the right to free expression, the right to reject a form of government and philosophy that was anti-human and anti-democratic. We were aware of the anti-Semitic foundation of Hitler's philosophy but we were not aware, as we could not be, of the inhuman and lunatic extent to which those philosophies were pursued.
The Holocaust to which the Prime Minister referred, that crime against humanity, could only be possible in a totalitarian state where the truth was kept from the people. At that time we perceived very dimly, it is true, the face of totalitarianism in the face of Naziism, but we perceived that neither could live in a world where freedom was cherished. The concept of freedom is based on an appreciation of the human personality.
Over vast regions of the earth today and throughout widely separated parts of the world, humanity is subjected to indignities and horrors which reveal that totalitarianism, the subjugation of the individual by the state, still lives and breathes. In police states where freedom depends on the colour of skin or racial origin, totalitarianism continues to hold sway. We fought in those days to push back the creeping incubus of totalitarianism and the crushing out of the human spirit. Since the end of the war in 1945, this day 40 years ago, it has been creeping forward. That is what the war then was about and that is why young Canadians went out to serve.
Last month during my visit to Europe to discuss NATO affairs, I could not help but remember the magnitude and magnificence of the effort made by those committed to the concept of freedom, by those committed to the conviction that totalitarianism has no place in any free society.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF VE DAY
speechtext:
So yes, Mr. Speaker, it was worth doing. To remember that is something that we owe to the members of that generation whose like we shall not soon see again. They went out with a smile on their lips to face death in a multitude of forms. They went out because they wanted a world in which children could play on the lawn of Parliament Hill and in which the divine spark of creation in every human being was respected. They went out because freedoms were at stake.
Those freedoms cannot be taken for granted. Every diligence is required by all Canadians in order to ensure the maintenance of their continued existence. It should be the dedication of all Canadians, not just that of those who lived and acted in those days, to show how easily the tragedy of war can be prevented, as World War II could have been prevented, and how the malice of the wicked is reinforced by the weakness of the virtuous, as was the case then and as should not be repeated.
We remember 40 years ago. We remember those who made possible our existence as we should be straining and are straining with every fibre of our being to see that war does not happen again.

subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF VE DAY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF VE DAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to respond to the excellent remarks which were made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and particularly to the very eloquent speech which was made by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) who spoke on behalf of the generation, both in this Chamber and throughout the country, which went to war. I want to salute him personally for his very remarkable war record and the Distinguished Flying Cross which he was awarded. It is no accident that he chose to wear that tie this afternoon and he is entitled to it.

subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF VE DAY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF VE DAY
speechtext:
I am sure the Deputy Prime Minister can recall the moment when he learned that the war in Europe had been declared over. It was one of the occasions in the lives of those of us who were living at that time when I am sure each of us remembers just what he or she was doing when the war's end was announced. I was in my final year of high school in Ottawa. Immediately the schools were let out and the whole city spontaneously moved to what is now called Confederation Square to celebrate with joy, pride and relief the ending of that terrible conflict.
Forty years and victory in Europe is at one time and the same time so very close over the millenium of human experience, yet so very far away. The names of Dieppe, Normandy, the campaign in Italy and the Netherlands will always be inscribed on the battleshields of our forces. We remember the valour, pride and suffering. In our gallery today there are some very distinguished representatives of our forces, including one of our very distinguished Field Commanders.

May 8, 1985
VE Day
A whole generation went to war and we are grateful to them. I want to assure the House that we shall not forget. We shall not forget our dead, those who threw the torch from failing hands, our wounded, and those men and women who, because of active service, have remained disabled for the past 40 years. Their lives have been curtailed and they have had to struggle against deep physical problems. In his absence, I also want to salute the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) who ably represents those men and women.

Mr. Speaker, the vast majority of Canadians were not even born 40 years ago, but for the hundreds of thousands who were, the sad memory is still alive of relatives and friends who fell at the front.
Mr. Speaker, I want to remind young Canadians that like the generations that went before, we must always be prepared to defend our freedom. Freedom is not something that just happens. We must fight for it continuously. During the two World Wars, two generations of Canadians left this country to fight for the cause of freedom.
Mr. Speaker, I would also mention that Canada came of age during the Second World War.

This nation came of age. We entered the war in 1939, primarily as a dispersed agricultural country. During the war we mobilized an unprecedented war effort. We became an industrial nation. Our high sense of unity and purpose during the war years has never been duplicated in the history of this country.
As a young boy, I can recall that my mother worked as a public servant in this town. I recall the hours which the men and women worked who were not fighting, but who came from all corners of Canada to contribute their services to mobilize the war effort. They gave this country standard, distinction and reputation world-wide. They gave Canada its current good standing in the world.

subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF VE DAY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF VE DAY
speechtext:
As we stand on a nuclear threshold, let us show fidelity to memory and truth. Let us acknowledge that human history is replete with examples of brutality and inhuman behaviour which result when bigotry, fear and hatred are allowed to guide governments or groups of individuals.
I can recall the fortieth anniversary of the Holocaust which took place on Parliament Hill ten days ago, a day when those memories were very, very vivid in the minds of those who survived those terrible moments and years. We must strive desperately for peace.
[ Translation]
Canada is privileged to be living in peace, protected from the physical and psychological ravages of war, but these are very agitated times we live in, and war continues to be a daily reality for millions of people throughout the world.

Let us realize that we enjoy the comforts, safety and peace of this country. That we must do because we have to maintain the determination, courage and will to meet the challenge of our times the way that an earlier generation met the challenge of those times. If we do not do that, then we will not, in fact, be keeping faith with those who made the ultimate sacrifice which we recall this afternoon. That sacrifice ended in victory, happily, 40 years ago today. We must keep that faith.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: COMMEMORATION OF FORTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF VE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) to say a few words on this important and historic anniversary.
Forty years ago, the Allies won final victory over Naziism in Europe. Today is a day for remembrance of that great achievement by the united citizens of many nations; it is a day for the celebration of the greatest popular victory of our times, and an occasion for reflection on where we stand in the world 40 years later.

The Second World War was unique because it was a genuine war of the people. We are not celebrating the victory of one group of nations against another, but the victory of democracy over fascism. It is important to remember that, in the battle for democracy, not only the Allies but also the people of occupied Europe were united, including those who fought courageously underground against the fascist powers in their countries.

VE Day opened up a new era of democratic possibility and promise. The aftermath of the war saw the successful establishment, not only of new democratic institutions throughout western Europe, but also of the beginning of the end of colonialism throughout the world.

Today, we ought to celebrate the fact that democracy is firmly rooted in Western Europe and that both victors and vanquished can celebrate the results of 40 years of democracy and friendship. Formerly victims of fascist rule, Germany, Italy, Spain and Portugal are now genuine democracies.
We must also remember today, Mr. Speaker, on this important anniversary, that the democratic nations achieved a victory in alliance with the Soviet Union, whose peoples experienced unimaginable horror. While we lament the fact that victory for democracy in 1945 was not completed in eastern Europe, we should recall, particularly in these very difficult international times, and recall with appreciation, the shared victory of the Canadian, European and other peoples
May 8, 1985

with the people of the Soviet Union in that historic battle against fascism.

Today, we should commemorate the tremendous contribution made by the Canadian people to the victory of democracy over Nazism. For five long years, Canadians fought spiritedly for a cause that revived and restored our own sense of identity and brought a new dimension to the national ideals we share. Above all, today is a day of commemoration of the ultimate sacrifice Canadian men and women made by giving their lives for freedom.

To remember the spirit of VE Day 40 years ago is to remember a sense of relief, as some Hon. Members who are a bit older than the rest of us have indicated here today, of pride in the achievements and sacrifices of Canadians and of all other members of the human family. They fought in one of the few just wars in history in order to procure freedom. Millions lost their lives.
I would like to conclude with the observation that it is up to our generation to honour those who died by using our talents and energy to extend freedom to all, and to take all the steps now necessary to head off another global conflict in the grim knowledge that such a conflict could be our last.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister will understand if we have to change the mood. He will know that the Chief Justice of the British Columbia Supreme Court recently ruled that the Government of British Columbia is in violation of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and of the Canada Health Act in its actions to restrict billing numbers for doctors.
I put the question to the Prime Minister in the absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The actions of the Government of British Columbia were described by the Chief Justice as "Orwellian", "draconian", and "the antithesis of fundamental justice". In an arrogant response to this judgment of the court, the Government of British Columbia has tabled Bill C-50, the Medical Services Amendment Act, which attempts to do what the Chief Justice said was illegal and against our Constitution. This Bill is a blatant violation of the
Oral Questions
rights of individuals, and a vicious assault on our national medicare system.
What will the Prime Minister, and his Ministers, do to respond to this blatant attempt by the Government of British Columbia to savage our national medicare system in that province?

Mr. Speaker, I regret the absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He would, no doubt, be able to provide a more specific response to my right hon. friend. I can, without commenting on what transpired in other jurisdictions, certainly acknowledge the legitimacy of any concerns which my right hon. friend may have in regard to our national health plan. I think on many occasions members of all Parties in this House have made firm their commitment to the integrity of the health care delivery services in this country which are so important to all of us. And I make that commitment again to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition today. The federal Government will maintain the integrity of that system at all times.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this situation has persisted for a month or two. The Government of British Columbia has introduced this Bill which, and I quote from one sentence in that Bill, "imposes limits on services and benefits available to different classes of insured persons". It goes right to the heart of our medicare system in trying to destroy it.
The federal Government should have already acted, in our opinion.
Hear, hear!

It is the responsibility of the Government of Canada to ensure and sustain the integrity of a national medicare system which the Prime Minister contends he supports. I ask the Prime Minister once more, would he instruct his Minister to take action in response to that particular piece of legislation, and use what weapons there are available under the Canada Health Act?

Mr. Speaker, my right hon. friend can receive the assurance that the Minister of National Health and Welfare will have been monitoring this situation, of course, very carefully. My right hon. friend is aware of his commitment to the values contained in the legislation which we have all defended here in the House of Commons.
In a federal state there is a matter of provincial jurisdiction in terms of it coming before the House of Commons-the manner in which it is raised. But I give my right hon. friend the assurance that we shall maintain the integrity of our much admired-and properly so-health care system in this country at all times.

May 8, 1985
Oral Questions
I would like to remind the Prime Minister that the Canada Health Act is a federal piece of legislation and he has a duty to defend it.

The House resumed from Tuesday, May 7, consideration of Bill C-30, an Act to amend the Bretton Woods Agreements Act and to repeal the International Development Association Act and amend certain other Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs; and Motion No. 2 (Ms. Jewett).

Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us today, Bill C-30, an Act to amend the Bretton Woods Agreements Act and to repeal the International Development Association Act and amend certain other Acts, is a very serious matter in the development field. The Bretton Woods Agreements, of course, arouse all of our highest expectations for aid by way of loans to the developing world. We are dealing today with an amendment which attempts to deal with some very serious problems in the actual functioning of world credit agencies at the present time.
The motion before us that Bill C-30 be amended in Clause 7 would require the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to provide a detailed review of Canada's participation in lending as a member of the World Bank group and the International Monetary Fund and, in particular-and I want to go through this in some detail-there are four criteria which would add considerably to the functioning of the World Bank group in order to have it achieve the objectives which were certainly set out in spirit for it. These criteria are: (a) Canada's use of its voice and vote to promote internationally recognized human rights; (b) Canadian initiatives to promote the use of loans to meet the basic human needs of the poorest and to provide for an equitable distribution of income in recipient countries; (c) policy actions taken by Canada to protect the neutrality and multilateral character of the World Bank group and International Monetary Fund and to resist the excessive pursuit of rigid bilateral policies by other member nations; and (d) Canadian initiatives to promote financial adjustment policies that do not impose additional hardship on the poor.
Why are these amendments needed, Mr. Speaker? Let us go to the issue of human rights. Canada's record on this issue is not particularly good. We have not opposed, for example, a loan to Chile, to a very repressive military dictatorship there, when even the United States Government abstained. Chile has one of the most atrocious records but even in this extreme case we failed to speak up on human rights issues. The demand here is that Canada use its opportunity and its vote to speak on these crucial loans in order to give better recognition to human rights issues.
Let me be clear as to what is meant by "internationally recognized human rights". We are not talking about an elaborate and difficult test of democratic rights. This is getting down to what is very, very minimal. Let me refer to what the Interchurch Task Force on the Churches and Corporate Responsibility have proposed as internationally recognized human rights. There are three points: freedom from arbitrary arrest, detention and execution; freedom from torture or cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment; and freedom from internal or external exile.
These are all perfectly obvious and it is quite clear that we are not talking about the imposition of certain democratic traditions or certain cultural expectations by our country on countries which do not have them and which, nevertheless, have their people in need of development aid and loans.
The second criterion is Canadian initiatives to promote the use of loans to meet the basic human needs of the poorest. It is necessary to specify this because, unfortunately, the very poorest countries are sometimes unable to get loans, and sometimes loans are used to divert resources and develop aspects of the economy which profit the better-off members of the country rather that the poorest. We must provide for an equitable distribution of income in recipient countries rather than merely promoting the strength of powerful groups within those societies, assisting them to get economic advantages which further entrench their power.
This money comes from public funds to which all Canadians have contributed. Canadian standards of decency and sharing should be respected in the according of loans, in so far as that is possible. I would like to make it very clear that the recommendation is that even in countries with bad human rights records, where the money is for the purpose of meeting basic human needs such as food and shelter, it should go to all people. Otherwise we should be demanding and encouraging respect, at least for these very basic human rights.
The third criterion deals with the issue of politicization. We do not want these funds to be politicized in any possible way. The amendment reads in part, "Policy actions taken by Canada to protect the neutrality and multilateral character of the World Bank group". This amendment arises from a number of very specific examples of abuses in the management of these funds. I refer particularly to American pressure to stop a loan to Nicaragua. This is in furtherance of American policy, which is an affair of the United States. However, the
May 8, 1985

International Monetary Fund and the World Bank are international multilateral agencies which gave different economic criteria. If those economic criteria are respected, that loan should have gone through.
If one is going to argue, as the United States has, that Nicaragua's abuse of human rights is so excessive that it should not get a loan, then we must ask why El Salvador, Honduras and South Korea are getting loans. Should there be a number of different standards depending upon the politics of the regime in question? If these countries can get loans it demonstrates that the human rights standards are not very good. To bar another country from getting loans by applying different standards is absolutely unacceptable. I am sorry to say that Canada did nothing to object to the dropping of the Nicaraguan loan. Canada did not protest.
The fourth matter, Canadian initiatives to promote financial adjustment policies that do not impose additional hardships on the poor, comes once again from hard experience. We have a number of recommendations from the Task Force on Churches and Corporate Responsibility. They refer to the long history of the International Monetary Fund imposing very severe conditions on debtor countries. The debtor countries must then cut back on Government expenditures. They may cut back on social, health and food expenditures. They have often been required to increase food prices. The result is great hardship for the poorest members of those countries.
The Interchurch Task Force recommended that social impact criteria be an integral part of the adjustment measures that are negotiated. In other words, when negotiations are ongoing, the country should be asked very specifically how different groups within that society would be affected by the various cut-backs that would be required. This process would ensure that the burden not fall as much as it has in the past on the poorest members of those countries. Unfortunately, this has not been the case before. These criteria must be spelled out concretely in order for them to be taken into account.
One of the results of the imposition of very severe measures in a country is that people resist. There have been food riots and other kinds of disturbances as a result of these repressive measures in very poor countries. Governments then have to react to that and there is an escalation of repression as a result of the imposition of what was supposed to be a measure of aid to the country in question.
The Task Force on Churches and Corporate Responsibility, which appeared before the standing committee, made a number of comments and very good recommendations on these various points. I would like to quote from their testimony on these basic issues. They refer to the social tensions which in turn have given rise to repression on the part of the state. The testimony reads in part as follows:
Where debtor countries are already ruled by repressive dictatorships, repression is often severely increased and potential for a return to democracy is diminished.
We therefore recommend to the members of the standing committee-
-and I recommend in turn in passing on these remarks, that the economic analyses and adjustment recommendations
Bretton Woods Agreements Act
should include a projection of the distribution relative to the income distribution of the debtor country.
The testimony continues:
Where such projection indicates that the main economic burden will fall upon those with the least income, adjustment measures should be revised to correct the balance and to safeguard the living standards of those most vulnerable.
These are extremely relevant words of counsel, Mr. Speaker. We want humane policies. We need specific criteria to change the rather sorry record we have had. I hope Hon. Members will support this motion of amendment to bring provisions into effect which would respect the humanitarian concerns that we all share.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support Motion No. 2 of the motions put before the House by the Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett). This set of amendments is designed to bring about more openness in government and to provide the recognition of parliamentary control of spending.
Motion No. 2 would make the permanent requirements part of the annual report. The annual report of an agency such as this is quite important because it presents the opportunity for the provision of a great deal of information about the agency and about the way in which Canada's role is being carried out in supplying moneys to the World Bank group, the International Monetary Fund, and related agencies. This amendment requires the annual report to spell out four or five definite items which would be reported on annually.
Some of the Government Members who spoke on Motions Nos. 1 and 2 seemed to think that the purpose of the motions was to provide an opportunity for Opposition Members to hold up the amendment of the Bretton Woods Agreements Act each time it came before Parliament. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, this amendment would provide a series of pertinent information in an annual report. In that way Members of Parliament would have that information available to them and would not have to use the guise of a parliamentary debate to attempt to get information concerning this particular agency. We would not have to force it into committee so that witnesses could be called and information could be gathered.
In addition to the information required by the amendment of the Government, our motion would require the inclusion of a small report on the use of Canada's voice and vote to promote internationally recognized human rights. That is something that coincides with international funding. Many cases have been outlined during this debate where the influence of some countries on the boards of these financial institutions has meant that moneys end up going to Goverments with repressive regimes that do not live up to the international requirements for the recognition of human rights. However, money is granted to those countries in any event. Therefore, I think it only fair that Canada should annually report its stand with respect to votes regarding loans to those kinds of regimes.

It is my hope that Government Members have seen the light, will understand the importance of annual and full reports and realize that it reflects their commitment to an open government that will keep citizens and parliamentarians fully informed.
Therefore, in terminating this debate, I hope Hon. Members will support this amendment so that information may be made available through an annual report rather than forcing the Opposition Parties to bring the Bretton Woods Agreements Act before committee to obtain this information at committee stage each time it comes before Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to speak very briefly on this Bill. The House will recall that when we discussed this issue some time ago, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Blais) made an address to the House indicating that he was informing Hon. Members that Canada had one of the Finest meat inspection systems in the world. Hon. Members on all sides of the House acknowledge that. At the time this issue was discussed previously, one Hon. Member across the way insinuated that Liberal Members were not of that view. Of course, that was utter nonsense. Liberal Members do in fact acknowledge that the meat inspection system in this country is indeed excellent.
In the speech he made, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture seemed to describe this Bill as though it contained a major new discovery and a major new area of policy. However, most of the things contained within this Bill are simply to ensure that the Act will conform to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. If one were to have read the speech as it was made by the Parliamentary Secretary without knowing better, one would have thought that the greatest thing ever to happen to agriculture would be the passage of Bill C-33.
When discussing in this House the entire issue of meat inspection, I think it is incumbent upon us to remind the Government across the way of what it is doing regarding inspection fees as they relate to the agricultural sector. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and, more particularly, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) are perpetrating an increase in these fees on the people of the country.
We all know that the agricultural industry is indeed in very serious difficulty. It is suffering and in general has fallen on very hard times. I see many Hon. Members across the way who are members of the Agriculture Committee as 1 am. Lately, the Finance Committee, which at the time was composed of most of the members of the Agriculture Committee, met in order to discuss the problems of farm financing. At that time we discovered that the farming industry is indeed in bad shape. I bring this to the attention of the House to indicate that the farm community is least able now to support major increases in inspection fees.
The Minister of Agriculture has told us that he has finally succeeded in coming to an agreement with a few commodity groups though not all of them. I frankly wonder how the Minister of Agriculture managed to come to this agreement. I suppose he probably said to the farmers: "You either take this agreement or you will not get anything else," and the farmers had to agree with him. I know that the farmers would have preferred seeing no increase in fees and no implementation of fees where they did not already exist. That is what the farming community really needs.
While discussing meat inspection, I think we must also seize this opportunity to talk about the whole problem not only of meat inspection but of meat imports. I see that the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Bissonnette) is sitting across from me. I know he is quite involved in agricultural matters
May 8, 1985

and I am sure the farmers of his constituency, like the farmers of my own, have discussed with him the very important issue of meat imports from the European Economic Community and, more particularly, those from Denmark and Ireland. These imports will very shortly be invading the Canadian market again at below the fair price.
Over the last three or four days, I have been receiving calls at the rate of about a dozen a day from the beef producers of my riding, each one asking me to voice the message to this Government that the beef farmers need to be protected. Of course, Mr. Speaker, you will probably tell me that that does not directly relate to the subject at hand, and perhaps you would be correct in so stating. However, we are discussing agriculture, the meat sector and inspection fees. I wonder if the Government would not consider a whole variety of measures to ensure that there is no unfair competition in the Canadian market-place caused by the subsidized imports invading our market. This unfairness is now compounded by the fact that Canadian farmers will have to pay higher inspection fees, thus making it more difficult for them to compete with imported products.
When we spoke of this Bill previously, I asked some questions regarding it. I hope I will still have the opportunity to find out about the state of certain clauses of this Bill and, more particularly, those that apply to the penalties for infractions against this piece of legislation. I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to tell us exactly what penalties will be imposed upon those who choose not to respect this new law.
As the Bill was originally drafted and presented in the House, offenders against the legislation would not have been subjected to jail terms, and that was specifically stated in the Bill. The concern that I had at that time, and that I still have to a certain extent, was the fact that the Bill almost contained an advertisement saying: "If you do not respect the law, do not worry about it because we cannot put you in jail anyway". I cannot help but feel that that is not a good signal to send out. It does not provide the kind of motivation necessary to ensure that the very good and stable reputation that our Canadian meat inspection system has enjoyed throughout all these years will continue.
1 am not saying that all people who are in the meat processing business are not trustworthy. That is not the case. Of course, most of them are good business people. The ones who are good business people want to ensure that the law is strong and powerful and that it protects them in case people entering the business are not as trustworthy as they are.
Again, we want to be assured that the law protects our good meat processing plants and mostly that the law protects the inspection system. The inspection system is what retains credibility in the fine products produced by our farmers and, more particularly, in the meat products that are stamped and have enjoyed throughout the years a high degree of credibility.
Those are the words I wished to put on the record regarding this Bill. To reiterate what I said in the beginning, I would like to remind the Parliamentary Secretary of the very lengthy and decided speech he made when this legislation was introduced.
Meat Inspection Act
In his speech, he almost claimed that he had written this legislation himself and that he had saved the farming industry by changing the meat inspection system to make it adhere to the Charter of Rights. Of course, the Bill does not do all the things the Parliamentary Secretary said it would do. However, we want to ensure that the Bill is as good as it can be in order to retain and protect the valuable and trusted meat inspection system which we have enjoyed in Canada for many years. Hopefully, we will enjoy that for many years to come.
Finally, I hope that the red meat industry, and more particularly the beef industry, will still be there. There will not be much to inspect unless the producers are protected from the foreign imports which I described a few minutes ago.

Mr. Speaker, what the House is doing today is the last parliamentary step in making the new meat inspection legislation of 1985 law. After this, it will simply have to be proclaimed by the Government and signed by the Governor General.
This Bill did nothing terribly radical. In fact, only one or two minor changes were made in this Bill that was taken from the three old Acts. The only difference is that it is now easier for people to check the law because it is written on one piece of paper. The new activity is not very radical. It simply spells out the procedure which a meat inspector will have to go through if he wishes to enter a dwelling house in order to get evidence or inspect meat which he feels is within his ambit. The inspector will now be required under the Charter of Rights to obtain a warrant for such an activity. That is a very minor change and probably it would have been upheld under the Constitution without the change being made to the legislation. Basically, we are left with a peice of paper which contains three laws.
The process did not receive a lot of debating time, nor did it deserve a lot of debating time. Members of Parliament, farmers, meat packers, processors and consumers are convinced

May 8, 1985
Meat Inspection Act
that we have the makings of a very good meat inspection system. If it is not the best in the world, it is certainly among the best in the world.
We heard witnesses in committee who were inspectors and we heard witnesses from the Canadian Meat Council, which represents 70 or 80 of the 530 or 540 meat processors whom we have in Canada. The Canadian Meat Council generally represents the larger of those operations. We also heard from departmental officials whose responsibility it is to carry out the inspection service.
In second reading debate it was noted that this law provides, in very broad terms, the power to the Ministry of Agriculture, and to the Minister of Agriculture in particular, to make regulations. It is the Minister of Agriculture and the Cabinet who will ultimately set out the regulations which will decide whether the high standards in the meat inspection service will continue or whether they will be downgraded. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) will decide whether the frequency of the inspection level program, which began under the last Minister of Agriculture, will continue, and whether the attitude under that program, which allows plants some discretion in the amount of time in which they will be inspected, should be extended further, or whether inspection periods should be relaxed.
The legislation gives responsibility to the Minister of Agriculture and the Cabinet to set the fees and charges for inspection services, whether the product is being imported or whether it is being inspected at the first slaughter or at the processing level. It also gives the Minister of Agriculture the responsibility to designate the various categories of plants and the establishment of standards for those categories.
Likewise, this Bill sets out who is the operator. In the process of hearing witnesses before the Standing Committee on Agriculture, we did not receive a particular definition of who would be considered to be the operator. That becomes very important with the new levels of penalties and fines which can be put into effect by the Minister of Agriculture. It begs the very serious question as to who is responsible if an inspector finds that someone in a plant is breaking the law. Is it the responsibility of the plant's management or the plant's ownership? How does the inspector trace whether the worker was simply carrying out a verbal order from head office or whether he was acting of his own volition? We will not know the answers to those questions until such time as inspectors take the cases to the courts. I hope the Minister of Agriculture and the Cabinet will tighten up those definitions in such a way as to permit the meat inspection regulations to be carried out so that the operator and owners of the plants will be made responsible for the way in which they instruct their workers to behave in those plants.
Basically, we have the same framework and guidelines which were set forward by Parliament for the meat inspection service to operate. We have given, and continue to give a great deal of discretionary powers to the Minister and the Ministry. I hope they continue to carry out those responsibilities in a fair manner and in the best interests of the farmers, processors,
workers in the processing plants and ultimately, the consumers who eat the meat. We are vesting a great deal of responsibility with the Minister of Agriculture. Parliament is passing the responsibility to the Minister and I wish him well in carrying out those responsibilities. I hope that he will continue, as have previous Ministers, to carry them out in the best interests of all Canadians.
