Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a couple of points concerning the difficulties which people in the Territories have experienced with meat inspection in the past. One problem which has occurred is the difficulty of shipping meat, particularly beef, from northern Alberta into the southern Territories. For instance, there were no federally-regulated slaughterhouses in the High Level area. Federal plants are located in the more southerly part of the province. So if one wanted to bring meat into the Territories across the provincial border, one had to bring it in from southern Alberta rather than from northern Alberta. That is a problem which caused us some concern.
Another problem was what to do with wild game products, particularly musk-ox. There is a lot of interest in the commerce in musk-ox meat, in buffalo, in reindeer and in caribou, and it is not possible in many circumstances to comply fully with the requirements of the Department of Agriculture. But there is no reason why that type of trade should not be engaged in. Of course, there has to be a system of some kind of inspection. Everyone knows that. But we might not be able to do that in a plant which meets all of the special requirements.
So I am pleased that in the Bill with which we are dealing today there is, in subsection 20(r), a provision for the exemption of certain of the requirements. I am sure that many of my constituents will be pleased to see that that provision is there and that the Governor-in-Council can make regulations pertaining to these exemptions so that in the future we will be able to bring in beef from northern Alberta and we will be able to encourage the trade in wild game meats.

Mr. Speaker, 1 also welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate, and I shall, if I may, express to the House a certain number of concerns. First of all, I think everyone will agree that our Canadian meat inspection system is one of the best if not the best in the world. Over the years, Canada has acquired an enviable reputation in this area, and the legislation before the House today may affect this well-deserved reputation, a reputation that has taken years to build up.
Everyone will also remember that not very long ago we had a rather embarrassing and even dramatic situation in Quebec,
May 8, 1985

and quite recently, the Quebec Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Garon, said:
I do not see why some people insist on having "Canada inspected" beef, since Quebec's inspection standards for beef are just as strict if not more so than Canada's.
When people think that "Canada approved" means that the standards are stricter, they are wrong. Standards are actually stricter in abattoirs built according to Quebec regulations.
We must have these standards to make a good product. We start with the proper conditions. We cannot produce a good product in a shack.
1 think this is a rather significant statement that shows even the Quebec Minister of Agriculture acknowledges the enviable reputation of our inspection system.
The purpose of the Bill may be entirely praiseworthy, and I support its objectives in principle, but practically speaking, I think the Bill is going to make for a relatively confusing situation and will, in the final instance, make the Canadian consumer feel pretty insecure. There may be something behind all this, and it is probably the Government's resolve, which it has demonstrated several times, to reduce spending, which in itself is important and entirely praiseworthy, except that I think 1 would like to consider for a moment what the consequences might be. I think that our reputation on local, provincial and foreign markets has gained ever wider currency over a number of years. This sector makes a very significant contribution to the Canadian economy. I would suggest that anything at all to do with inspection must remain under Government jurisdiction, and I find it hard to believe that our inspection system will ever so slowly be dismantled piece by piece so that it will eventually be taken over by private interests.
The ultimate aim of this inspection process would likely become rather fuzzy if people were to question our objectivity, and 1 think that consumers and buyers of our products would rightfully express doubts about our standards, which in turn would be considerably lessened. That is why I fail to see the rationale behind a measure such as Bill C-33 which, in a way, will lead to insecurity and confusion, when we are talking about a sector that is running very smoothly and that has gained wide-ranging acceptance.
The private sector is here to stay, of course, it has earned its laurels and, oftentimes, private enterprise will give much better results than will any public agency. But when we are talking about security and consumer protection, I do think that the Government must play a leading role and resort to every means at its disposal to improve consumer protection mechanisms.
I am not at all sure that, from a structural standpoint, results will not be short of disastrous. If I may, I should like to mention some of the consequences which, I think, might result from the implementation of this Bill. What guarantee do we have that this will not result in an inadequate control over quality inspection and appraisement of meat and meat products? 1 am almost certain there will be an immediate reduction
Meat Inspection Act
in inspection standards. Probably, there will also be a definite drop in the quality of all food products, especially meat products. Most certainly, there will also be a lowering of sanitary conditions in industries. Clearly, there will also be inadequate control over meat and meat product receiving or shipping. I am not sure there will also not be inadequate monitoring of the preparation of processed meat products. There will certainly be a quality decline in the production of processed meat preparations, a lack of control over the export of meats and meat products.
I could go on and on and show that our success on the markets has been due definitely to the reputation we developed over the years, our excellent reputation in terms of extremely drastic standards. At this important juncture, where we do have as great a need for our agro-food economy as ever, it seems to me both ill-advised and extremely dangerous to tamper with anything that has proven effective.
Let me tell you that meat processing is the major manufacturing industry in many provinces, and the fourth one nationally in terms of shipping value. This in itself is the most convincing proof that here is an industry that is vital to the Canadian economy.
Also, the Canadian Government has contributed over these last few years to the expansion and growth of this industry, not through direct intervention on the market place, but rather by supporting the infrastructure that links the various components, which allowed Canada to enjoy a respected worldwide position as a supplier of meat.
The help provided by Agriculture Canada in the carcass grading system also served Canadians well in the industry, because it has provided them with a quality product that is still envied in the world at large.
Such are my concerns, Mr. Speaker, and I very sincerely believe that Bill C-33 could threaten the objectivity of a system that has proven itself over the years. The whole aspect of consumer protection, the concern for consumers has been left aside. In other terms, they have been completely ignored, although the vivid recollection of past experience still raises fears, and I am referring of course to the situation we have experienced in Quebec. Under the circumstances, it seems to me very dangerous to give the Minister absolute, unrestricted control over an area as important as our meat market.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions, comments, debate. The Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre).

Thank you Mr. Speaker. 1 also welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on second reading of Bill C-33, respecting meat inspection in Canada. I am especially pleased to see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Blais), in the absence of the Minister, because the Parliamentary Secretary

May 8, 1985
Meat Inspection Act
made a very eloquent speech, and I would like to ask him to congratulate the public servant who wrote it for him. However, I must add that the officials who wrote this elegant prose may have forgotten to inform the Parliamentary Secretary that Bill C-33, which was based on very worthy principles-and who is not for virtue and motherhood-and I think the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Bissonnette), who, I am sure, is very familiar with this area, could tell us that the objectives of the Bill are praiseworthy, and I think that Hon. Members on both sides of the House agreed that the Bill, also thanks to Hon. Members on the Standing Committee, is well drafted.
I think the Minister of State for Small Businesses is referring to the Committee on Agriculture, and of course as the critic for external trade, I do have other obligations and I have to rely on the experts. Unfortunately, I am just a country lawyer, and I have not had the honour and the privilege of being involved in the agricultural industry like the Minister of State for Small Businesses. However, Mr. Speaker, I do know that under all the praiseworthy principles, the reality is not as rosy. With all its principles, the Government is in fact undermining the intrinsic value of the Canadian inspection service.
It is common knowledge that as a result of a policy referred to as the reduced inspection system or inspection frequency, the Government is undermining the whole credibility of "Canada Approved". This concern is shared by the inspectors themselves, who have to live with the practical implications of Bill C-33. I would like to remind the Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister that even the Canadian Meat Council said not long ago, I think it was on June 13 last year, that Canadians depended on Agriculture Canada's help in providing a system of carcass grading, and so on, and the Council said: Although we understand that the Federal Government is going through a difficult period financially, and that it is looking at every way it could possibly save money, we must also understand that meat inspection, grading services, and the like, are in the national interest and must continue to be financed from the public purse.
This is the reason why, Mr. Speaker, I would like to stir up the interest of my good friend, the Parliamentary Secretary, and congratulate him for his work. Nonetheless I would like to obtain his assurance that once this legislation is passed it will not be shelved but that indeed it will be enforced and even extended if possible. It would be terrible to alter among other things the various groups, the A, B, and C assessment system advocated for processing plants for example, when we know that the Department wants to compel all plants in the C group to pass in the B group thus reducing inspection services and in the short term to compel all plants in the B group to move into the A group thus reducing the inspection. In the end, the industries are entrusted with the responsibilities of sanitation and inspection. In fact, the concern which has been expressed, especially by inspectors, is that this could pose a very serious
danger for the Canadian public. I would like the Parliamentary Secretary to assure us that this Parliament is not being used only to pass a Bill which will not be actually implemented. I know very well, Mr. Speaker, that you would not be happy yourself to witness passage of a Bill which would not be actually implemented. As you know, we all feel very safe when we see the "Canada Approved" stamp on a cut of meat, and if this stamp were to be used without any effective control, it could become very worrying for consumers. The inspectors therefore met last weekend to express their concerns to some of our colleagues, and they took due note of the absence of 25 of the 26 Progressive Conservative Members they had invited. I think there will be other opportunities in the next few weeks to hear the same inspectors express their concerns and I hope that, before asking us to agree to this Bill, the Parliamentary Secretary will take all their grievances into consideration. They are the most knowledgeable in this area. For our part, we can certainly talk about the principle of the legislation, on which everyone agrees. However, as far as the actual administration of the act is concerned, the revelations of Agriculture Canada inspectors are disquieting, Mr. Speaker. For instance, they say that, if this policy is pursued, the quality control and assessment of meat and meat products through inspection will be inadequate. They say that inspection standards are about to be lowered. They even say that the quality of all food products, especially meat, will be lower. I know this is of particular concern to the Minister of State for Small Businesses.
I am convinced that the possibility of lower health standards within the industry is also of concern to the Parliamentary Secretary. Should the lack of control over the shipping and delivery of meat and meat products not give the Parliamentary Secretary something to think about? I think that no one would tolerate a lack of control over the preparation of processed meat. Mr. Speaker, who would accept lower quality control in the production of processed meat preparations? It is therefore my view that no one would agree to any lack of control over the export of meat and meat products.
Mr. Speaker, I think-the Minister of State for Small Businesses is telling me I have said that three times already-I will have to repeat it again and again in order to get him to understand. This is worrying all those involved in the area of inspection. They know very well that the Minister of State for Small Businesses, despite all his good will, did not understand their brief.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that inadequate control over imported meat products is also a genuine concern for inspectors. Worse still, they are telling us that this could lead to no control at all on stamped meat and meat products. If this were to happen, 1 think our stamp would lose much of its credibility, for it is now well looked upon not only across Canada but around the world. We are even warned about a sharp decline in the nutritional
May 8, 1985

value of meat and meat products. Imagine that! I hope there is nothing in that legislation that could bring about such nefarious results.
Mr. Speaker, there is even the prediction of a significant increase in black market operations. I know that no Member of this House could support such practices.
Of course, we are told consumers should be on the alert, we are told that if the process is allowed to continue, there may be a significant increase in the volume of meat and meats products on the market unsafe for human consumption.
Mr. Speaker, we have all lived through the times when tainted meat was sold openly, we were very concerned about the findings of some Quebec commissions of inquiry, and nobody would like to see a return to such dark days in the history of Quebec's food industry. Unfortunately, those incidents were attributed to the private sector, which the Minister holds in such high esteem.
They were Liberals.
I think the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) should continue to read his documents instead of indulging in petty politics, it would be of great help to him when he has to answer questions.
A flashback to history.

You know, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Communications keeps interrupting me because he knows that if any such thing were to happen again he would be blamed for failing to take part in today's debate.
Meat inspection services are of course reduced and finally we are informed by meat inspectors of the danger of the situation because the Canadian public is less protected in an environment described as open to fraud. And I know that the Parliamentary Secretary would never want that to happen. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would like the Parliamentary Secretary to dispel all those concerns before we have the final vote on this bill because we . . . This bill was not drafted by people who were unaware of the situation; this information came directly from the inspectors involved. This is why I am anxious to get assurances from the Parliamentary Secretary before a vote is called on a bill of such significance to the Canadian consumer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions. Comments. The Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif).

Mr. Speaker, I wish to confirm what was said by my colleague, the Hon. Member from Shefford (Mr. Lapierre). During the weekend, I attended a meeting in Notre-Dame-du-Bon-Conseil with about forty people who work in areas covered by this legislation. Forty persons who wanted to meet with their elected representatives, something quite
Meat Inspection Act
normal in my opinion. They wanted to meet the members from ridings which are mostly rural.
To my surprise, Mr. Speaker, out of 26 invitations, including the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais), the Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Vincent), only one Conservative showed up. This is an important question, and the people working in the field, who have the best possible knowledge and expertise of the application of such a legislation, wanted to meet their elected representatives to inform them of the possible, or even probable, consequences of the legislation. They were told that it is none of their business. All they wanted to do was warn the Members of the possible dangers of such legislation. That is the attitude of the Minister of State, the attitude of the Parliamentary Secretary. They draft a bill which, in theory, might be excellent, but which is in fact very dangerous for the Canadian consumers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Debate. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Blais).

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will take me 30 seconds to reply to my hon. colleague. Instead of having lunch with the meat inspectors in the Quatre Saisons Motel in Drummondville, the Hon. Members for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) and for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) would have been better advised to appear before the Standing Committee where I heard representatives of the meat industry as well as representatives of their party and of the New Democratic Party who did agree with me.
But I am now somewhat surprised to see that they seem to have changed their minds this afternoon. You may be sure, Mr. Speaker, and the opposition can be sure as well regarding the main concern of the meat inspectors whom the hon. members met but who actually invited me 48 hours in advance. I am not sure that they sent a letter of invitation to everybody for their meeting and even though I am not such an important person, I still expect to receive my invitations early enough. As I said, they had the opportunity to state their concern and they suggested that they were worried about their jobs. We provided them with figures showing that their jobs were not at stake at all and that we were simply streamlining the industry, something that has not been done since 1905. 1 believe now that at this very moment everybody supports that legislation and that we must go ahead with it, Mr. Speaker. I suggest that meat inspectors will carry on their work so as to preserve a reputation that Canada has had for years in that area and that we will continue to enjoy for years to come.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say briefly to the Parliamentary Secretary how pleased 1 am that he was able to assure us that no jobs are at stake, that in fact it is strictly a matter of streamlining the industry and that inspection standards will be as good as they have been since 1905.

May 8, 1985
Meat Inspection Act
However, I would like to point out to the Parliamentary Secretary that he should not blame Hon. Members for not sitting on the Standing Committee of Agriculture. The Parliamentary Secretary should understand that within our party, we have a right to speak whatever the opinion of our colleagues may be. I can assure him that nobody could prevent me from making representations on the floor of the House on behalf of the constituents of my riding of Shefford. I know that the Hon. Member has not enjoyed the same kind of right since he entered politics, Mr. Speaker. The Parliamentary Secretary should know that on this side of the House, even when we were sitting on the other side, we were never afraid to express our views on behalf of our constituents, and that is my main concern, not the commitments of the Parliamentary Secretary.

I have a question for the Parliamentary Secretary. While we are not able to ask questions directly of him or of the Minister, 1 have a question that arises from the testimony during the committee process. This matter has disturbed me since before the committee process when the new frequency of meat inspection was instituted approximately a year ago.
The Parliamentary Secretary will know that under that program the meat inspector is responsible for the stamp that goes on the meat carcass. However, with the new frequency of inspection, employees in some plants are apparently applying those stamps under the aegis of the inspector even though he may not be there because of his responsibility for inspecting several other plants.
Should the meat that bears the stamp be found wanting at a future date, who is responsible? Is it the plant operator, is it the employees, or is it the inspector? It is our understanding that the inspectors will be held responsible, but their instructions from the Department make it virtually impossible for them to be on hand to inspect the use of those stamps. Is the Department proposing any regulations to make this procedure more fair to the inspectors as well as to the consumers of Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a question of liability. My hon. friend knows that this problem was dealt with in the standing committee. Dr. Anzengruber had the responsibility of answering for the Department on this question.
It is impossible to say what will happen in a month or two if such a problem arises or to know exactly who has the responsibility.
We will see at that time. It is a very hypothetical question for which we had no answer and Dr. Anzengruber answered the best way he could at that time.
As our colleagues, the Hon. Members for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) and for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) have indicated earlier, we have trusted for many years our inspectors and our inspection system. We cannot either solve all the problems of the world, today, but we will attempt to respond-
What kind of response is that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Of course, had he been present earlier, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) would perhaps know. I cannot start over again every five minutes, each time someone enters the House. All I can say is that the Government will take on its responsibilities in this area as it did in the past and should a particular problem occur and should we have to determine whether the inspector or the company is responsible for some damage, we shall investigate and the responsible person or organization will pay the bill, which I suggest, is the normal thing to do.

Mr. Speaker, we had a reputation of passive spectators but we are now faced with representations of very silent mummies when it comes to defending the consumer's interests.
I have a question for the Parliamentary Secretary. If this legislation is so open, why did 26 members of your party refuse to meet with those people who work in the field? That is the first question.
Second, should an institution which is now controlled seven hours a day, five days a week be controlled one hour a day, five days a week, because in my opinion, inspection means control, and when there is less control, there is less inspection as well and we are now substantially diluting the meaning of "Canada Approved".

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Parliamentary Secretary has the floor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Regarding the first question asked by the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif), he could put it directly to the 26 members when he meets them. As for me, 1 said why I was not there. I had been invited two days in advance and I had the opportunity to meet those inspectors here in Parliament when they had the opportunity to explain their position.
As for the second part of the question, Mr. Speaker, I cannot make an analysis of the hundreds and the thousands of businesses working in the meat sector in Canada today; it is absolutely impossible to take specific cases, and my honourable friend knows it full well. The departmental officials have answered all the questions, to the satisfaction of the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), one of your colleagues and a member of your own party. He expressed his agreement on the legislation, on the guarantees given to him by the departmental officials about the follow-up to this Bill. I cannot elaborate further today, I refer hon. members to the guaran-
May 8, 1985

tees given in committee. It is pointless to set up standing committees and have them sit for days to study a legislation if we are to take up the whole debate again in this House, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) on a supplementary question.

Mr. Speaker, as far as I know, when we have to pass legislation, it is here in this House of Commons that it is to be done. I would like to ask the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary a question since he claims to be on top of the issue. Could he tell this House how many packing plants and processing plants there are in Quebec? Since he knows all the facts of the matter, those are figures he must certainly know-

speechtext: The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary.

speechtext: My hon. colleague can put his question on the Order Paper. I will enquire and I give him an answer in the next few days, Mr. Speaker.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. If I recall, the Parliamentary Secretary indicated earlier, in answer to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif), when he asked to what extent the system would be damaged by the fact that inspectors would not be on the premises as often as previously, that he could not deal with that hypothetical question at the present time, and that he would deal with the case when an infraction occurred. Does he not think that the inspection system, which he praised in his recent speech, saying that it was very good, which it is, does he not think that it will be damaged by the action of the government?
